heard: An amateur telescope can spot a quasar 2.4 billion light years away. Cataloged in the third Cambridge catalog as 3C273, this enigmatic object baffled astronomers for years. In 1963, astronomer Martin Schmidt calculated its massive redshift and revealed its true distance. It was identified as the very first quasar ever discovered in the universe. Powered by a supermassive black hole at the center of an elliptical galaxy in Virgo, it shoots out a 200,000-light-year jet. At visible wavelengths, it shines over 4 trillion times more luminous than the sun. And that mind-boggling power is why an amateur telescope can spot a quasar 2.4 billion light-years away.
